clue.text: Scrooge, say, before this is sung in church

parts.note: Dickens's Ebenezer Scrooge is the classic example of a miser
ere is an old word for before

explanation.surface: A remark that something is sung in church just ahead of a miserly character's arrival.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scrooge, say' names an example, so it gives the general word MISER; 'before' is not a placement signal but the old word ERE.
explanation.definitionFit: The Miserere is Psalm 51, a penitential psalm regularly sung or chanted in church services.

clue.text: Is post first-class up in Egypt?

parts.note: post and mail are the same thing

indicators.note: up in a down clue means the letters are read from bottom to top

parts.note: A1 means first-class, written AI in crosswords

explanation.surface: A query whether letters get sent at top rate somewhere in Egypt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns AI into IA at the end. The definition 'in Egypt' describes the answer as a place there.
explanation.definitionFit: Ismailia is a city on the Suez Canal, in north-eastern Egypt.

clue.text: Keen thin sauce — it's well mixed

indicators.note: well mixed tells the solver to stir the letters of thin sauce and it's into a new order

explanation.surface: A gravy that is too watery, but at least it has been thoroughly stirred.
explanation.definitionFit: Enthusiastic describes someone eager or full of zeal.

clue.text: Weird in old age — rich, we hear

parts.note: eld is an archaic word for old age

indicators.note: we hear signals that the next word is taken by its sound, not its spelling

parts.note: the word said aloud is rich

explanation.surface: A remark that wealth in one's later years is strange.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' is a link; 'we hear' turns 'rich' into the sound RITCH placed after ELD.
explanation.definitionFit: Eldritch is a Scots word for something unearthly or eerie.

clue.text: "March, march, — and Liddesdale" with Scott's Blue Bonnets

definitions.text: "March, march, — and Liddesdale" with Scott's Blue Bonnets

parts.words: "March, march, — and Liddesdale" with Scott's Blue Bonnets
parts.note: a quotation with a word missing, from Walter Scott's song Blue Bonnets over the Border, whose line names two Border valleys

explanation.surface: A line from a stirring Scottish marching song with a gap to fill.
explanation.walkthrough: Scott's line runs 'March, march, Eskdale and Liddesdale'; the answer fills the gap, naming a valley in the Scottish Borders.
explanation.definitionFit: The missing word is a Border dale through which the River Esk flows, named alongside its neighbour in the song.

clue.text: Ancient character loses heart in southern resort

indicators.note: loses heart means the middle letters of the resort's name are taken away

parts.note: Brighton is a seaside resort on England's south coast

explanation.surface: An old figure feels dispirited while staying at a seaside town in the south.
explanation.walkthrough: 'loses heart' removes GH, the middle two letters of BRIGHTON.
explanation.definitionFit: Ancient Britons were the Celtic people of Britain before the Romans, characters from early history.

clue.text: Fiery lawyer under the Stuarts?

parts.note: a hot-tempered jurist of the Jacobean age, also read as a fuel that burns hot

explanation.surface: A firebrand legal mind serving the Stuart kings.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir Edward Coke was a combative Chief Justice under James I; coke is also the fuel made from coal, which burns fiercely.
explanation.definitionFit: Coke is a fuel giving intense heat, and the surname of the great Stuart-era jurist.

clue.text: Badly needs fat to be secure

indicators.note: badly suggests the letters of needs fat are put in poor order and must be rearranged

explanation.surface: A complaint that someone desperately requires fat to stay safe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to be' is a link; 'secure' is the adjective, meaning fixed in place.
explanation.definitionFit: Something fastened is fixed firmly in place, so it is safe and held tight.

clue.text: Take girl to Georgia in America

parts.note: Sara is a girl's name
GA is the postal abbreviation for the US state of Georgia

explanation.surface: Someone is told to escort a young woman down to Georgia in the United States.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take' is an instruction to the solver, and the definition 'in America' describes the answer as a place found in the USA.
explanation.definitionFit: Saratoga Springs is a town in New York State, scene of a famous Revolutionary War surrender.

clue.text: Stomach's rejected a bit of dirt

indicators.note: rejected suggests something thrown back, so the word is read backwards

parts.note: tum is an informal word for the stomach; with the 's it gives tums

explanation.surface: An upset belly refuses a small piece of grime.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rejected' turns TUMS round to make SMUT.
explanation.definitionFit: Smut is a flake of soot or a speck of grime.

clue.text: Made thirteen, rebuilding real property

indicators.note: rebuilding puts the letters of made thirteen together in a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Someone makes thirteen while renovating a house.
explanation.definitionFit: In law a hereditament is any property, especially land or buildings, that can be inherited.

clue.text: Deplorable hazard below the motorway causes accident

indicators.note: below in a down clue places the following letters under the motorway piece

parts.note: the M1 is Britain's first motorway, written MI in crosswords
deplorable can mean sad
to hazard is to venture

explanation.surface: A terrible danger beneath a motorway bridge leads to a crash.
explanation.walkthrough: The M1 is the motorway from London to Yorkshire, written MI. 'below' stacks SAD and VENTURE under it in this down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: A misadventure is a mishap; death by misadventure is an accidental death.

clue.text: Little room — shut it after I left

parts.note: to shut is to close

indicators.note: left here means departed, so the letter I goes away from the word it

parts.note: taken as written before the deletion

explanation.surface: An order to close a small room once the speaker has gone out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I left' means the letter I leaves IT, so only T follows CLOSE; 'after' is a link placing it.
explanation.definitionFit: A closet is a small private room or cupboard.

clue.text: Puts off the ship one who is no sailor

definitions.text: Puts off the ship one who is no sailor

parts.words: Puts off the ship one who is no sailor
parts.note: a person who sets someone ashore, read as lands a man, combined with a description of someone who lives on dry ground rather than at sea

explanation.surface: A crew sets ashore a passenger who has never been to sea.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Puts off the ship one' reads as LANDS a MAN, while the rest describes a person who is no seaman.
explanation.definitionFit: Sailors' slang calls a person who lives and works on shore, with no experience at sea, a landsman.

clue.text: Criticize a S American's revolutionary's. swaggering style

parts.note: to pan a play is to criticize it harshly
Che Guevara was the Argentine-born revolutionary

explanation.surface: A critic attacks the flamboyant manner of a South American rebel.
explanation.definitionFit: Panache is flamboyant confidence or dash in manner.

clue.text: Architectural feature, the ultimate in masonry support

indicators.note: in signals that the ultimate word is placed inside the support word

parts.note: a pier is a pillar of masonry supporting an arch or bridge
the ultimate means the last

explanation.surface: A building detail presented as the best kind of stonework prop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the ultimate in masonry' looks like praise, but it puts LAST inside PIER.
explanation.definitionFit: A pilaster is a flat rectangular column projecting from a wall as decoration.

clue.text: It's intended to be read

explanation.surface: A note saying that something is meant to be looked at.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It's' and 'to be' are links between the two senses.
explanation.definitionFit: A studied remark is a deliberate one, and to have studied a subject is to have read it at university.

clue.text: Goes slow to deceive the French

parts.note: to trick someone is to deceive them
les is the French plural word for the

explanation.surface: Someone dawdles in order to fool the French.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to' is a link between the definition and the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Water that trickles moves slowly in a thin stream.

clue.text: Seven-nil somehow cheers one up

indicators.note: somehow suggests the letters of seven-nil are put together in some new way

explanation.surface: A seven-nil win in some way lifts a supporter's spirits.
explanation.definitionFit: To enliven someone is to make them livelier or brighter in mood.

clue.text: Burglar Bill accepts initially the royalties for hits

indicators.note: accepts means the burglar's name takes the other letters inside it

parts.note: Bill Sikes is the housebreaker in Dickens's Oliver Twist

indicators.note: initially picks the opening letter of each of the words the royalties

explanation.surface: A thief agrees to take the first share of royalties for his popular songs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'accepts' puts TR, the first letters of 'the royalties', inside SIKES; 'for' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Strikes are blows, so the word is a synonym for hits.

clue.text: Lost Pat's letters when making a call

indicators.note: letters asks for the letters of the phrase Lost Pat's to be rearranged, keeping the s

explanation.surface: Pat's mislaid mail turns up while someone is phoning.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe in 'Pat's' is ignored, so its S counts among the eight letters shuffled.
explanation.definitionFit: The Last Post is the bugle call sounded at military funerals and at the close of day.

clue.text: Love the symbol for this life supporter

definitions.text: Love the symbol for this life supporter

parts.words: Love the symbol for this life supporter
parts.note: love is the letter O in tennis scoring, and O is also the chemical symbol for the gas we breathe

explanation.surface: Someone adores the emblem of whatever keeps them alive.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue says that O, which stands for love (nil), is the chemical symbol of the element needed for life.
explanation.definitionFit: The element with chemical symbol O is the gas that animals breathe to stay alive.

clue.text: Thoughts about money standards

indicators.note: about means going around, so the thoughts word surrounds the money letter

parts.note: thoughts are ideas
L is the abbreviation for pound, the sign for money

explanation.surface: Musings on monetary benchmarks.
explanation.definitionFit: Ideals are standards of perfection one aims to meet.

clue.text: Hold fast and still outside Scottish port in difficult situation

parts.note: to hold fast is to stick

indicators.note: outside means the yet word surrounds the name of the port

parts.note: and still means and yet
Wick is a harbour town in Caithness, north-east Scotland

explanation.surface: Someone clings on and waits by a Scottish harbour in a tight spot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'outside' wraps YET round WICK to make YWICKET after STICK. A sticky wicket is a cricket pitch drying after rain, hard to bat on.
explanation.definitionFit: Taken from cricket, a sticky wicket is any awkward predicament.

clue.text: One of a number in Olivia's inventory

explanation.surface: A single article from a list of a woman's possessions.
explanation.walkthrough: In Twelfth Night Olivia mockingly lists her beauty as an inventory: 'item, two lips indifferent red; item, two grey eyes'.
explanation.definitionFit: An item is one entry in a list, and Olivia's catalogue of her features begins each line with this word.

clue.text: Handled by American journalist

parts.note: ED, short for editor, is the usual crossword journalist

explanation.surface: A matter dealt with by a reporter from the States.
explanation.walkthrough: The OCR dropped 'journalist', which gives ED.
explanation.definitionFit: Something handled has been put to use or employed.

clue.text: Look at part of telescope

parts.note: an instruction to examine one component, also read as the component that the eye looks through

explanation.surface: A request to examine one piece of a telescope.
explanation.definitionFit: The lens at the viewer's end of a telescope, against which you hold your eye, is the eyepiece.

clue.text: Anxiety many suffered at Tyburn

explanation.surface: The dread felt by crowds at an old London execution site.
explanation.walkthrough: Tyburn was London's chief place of public hanging until 1783, so those executed there suffered suspension from the rope.
explanation.definitionFit: Suspense is tense uncertainty, and also the state of being hung up, as the hanged were.
